planting.note: Plant divisions on a mossy log, bark mount, or shallow well-drained pot in partial to full shade after frost danger passes; the creeping rhizome should sit on or just under the surface, never buried deeply, since it roots and spreads along the top of its growing medium.

directions: Creeping felt fern is a small Southeast Asian and Pacific epiphyte that spreads by a thin, wiry, felt-scaled rhizome bearing single, round to oval, coin-shaped fronds a half-inch to an inch across, giving it a distinctly different look from the larger, tongue-shaped fronds of its relative Pyrrosia lingua. It roots into bark, mossy logs, rock crevices, or shallow pots of fast-draining epiphytic mix, forming a dense, low mat that is equally at home climbing a humid greenhouse wall or draping from a hanging basket. Let the surface dry slightly between waterings, since the fuzzy brown rhizome scales are prone to rot in constantly soggy conditions, and provide bright indirect light to partial shade rather than deep shade for the densest frond cover. Propagate by cutting and pinning rhizome sections onto fresh mounting material.
sources: American Fern Society -- Pyrrosia species in cultivation

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade after the last frost; this fern comes from cool, damp forest floors and resents drying out at the root.

directions: Hairy shield fern is a New Zealand and eastern Australian woodland native named for the fine, reddish-brown hairs that densely cover its stipes and rachises, a textural detail that distinguishes it at a glance from the smoother-stemmed Lastreopsis microsora. Its finely divided, dark green, triangular fronds arise from a slowly creeping rhizome to form a spreading colony rather than a tight clump, making it a good filler fern beneath tree ferns or larger shrubs in a cool, sheltered shade garden. It needs consistently moist, humus-rich soil and protection from drying wind and hot afternoon sun, performing best in maritime or high-humidity climates similar to its native range. Divide congested colonies in spring to propagate and to keep the planting from overcrowding.
sources: New Zealand Plant Conservation Network -- Lastreopsis hispida
Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria -- Lastreopsis species

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in warm, humid partial to full shade after all frost danger has passed; the thick, creeping rhizome's dense golden wool is a key ornamental feature and should not be buried.

directions: Golden chicken fern is a slow-growing Southeast Asian tree-fern relative whose thick, creeping, trunk-like rhizome is densely covered in long, shaggy, golden-brown hairs, a feature so striking that dried, shaped specimens gave rise to the medieval European legend of the 'Vegetable Lamb of Tartary,' a mythical plant-animal hybrid. Large, arching, bipinnate-to-tripinnate fronds rise from the woolly rhizome to form a dramatic architectural crown reminiscent of a true tree fern, though it reaches only a fraction of their eventual height. It demands warm temperatures, high humidity, and consistently moist, rich, well-drained soil, and resents cold drafts or dry air, making it best suited to sheltered tropical gardens or a warm greenhouse outside its hardiness range. The rhizome hairs and starchy pith have a long history of use in traditional Chinese medicine, where the plant is known as gou ji. Propagate by division of the rhizome or from spores.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens -- Cibotium barometz
American Fern Society -- Cibotium species in cultivation

planting.note: Plant divisions in well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade after frost danger passes; this fern spreads by creeping underground rhizomes and tolerates more dryness and open light than most ferns once established.

directions: Lacy ground fern is an Australian woodland species that forms loose colonies of finely divided, pale to mid-green, lacy-textured fronds rising from slender, far-creeping underground rhizomes, giving it a softer, airier texture than the coarser Dennstaedtia punctilobula already common in temperate gardens. In its native eucalypt forests it grows in dappled light along banks and gullies, and it carries that adaptability into cultivation, tolerating brighter, more open shade and shorter dry spells once its rhizome network is established than most woodland ferns. Use it as an informal, spreading groundcover beneath trees or large shrubs in a naturalistic shade garden, where its colonizing habit fills in bare ground readily. Divide and replant rhizome sections in spring to propagate or to control its spread into unwanted areas.
sources: Australian National Botanic Gardens -- Dennstaedtia davallioides profile
PlantNET (Royal Botanic Garden Sydney) -- Dennstaedtia davallioides

planting.note: Mount divisions on a bark slab or tree-fern fiber plaque lined with sphagnum, or pot in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic mix, in warm, humid partial to full shade after frost danger passes; the wiry, scaly, climbing rhizome clings to its support and should not be buried in soil.

directions: Scaly climbing fern is a Southeast Asian and Malesian rainforest epiphyte whose wiry, densely brown-scaled rhizome creeps and climbs over tree trunks and mossy rocks, bearing simple, undivided, leathery, lance-shaped fronds spaced singly along its length rather than the divided fronds typical of most ferns -- a form that gives the genus its name, from a resemblance to oleander leaves. It is best mounted on bark or a fern-fiber plaque where the climbing rhizome can grip and spread naturally, kept consistently humid and watered by soaking or misting rather than grown in standing wet soil. Native to humid lowland and montane rainforest understory, it wants warm, stable temperatures and protection from direct sun, which scorches the thin fronds. Propagate by cutting the rhizome into rooted sections and pinning each onto fresh mounting material.
sources: American Fern Society -- Oleandra species in cultivation
